summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency and throughput requirements for Lattice Retail. Customer needs sub-300ms p95 for short completions, streaming for token-by-token UX, and capacity to handle bursts to 400 concurrent users (approx 3k reqs/min). Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, KV/prefix caching, batching, quantization and benchmarking plan.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-21 14:30 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Meeting ID: ff-20260421-09a7
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Aaron Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Lattice Head of ML), Miguel Torres (Lattice Platform Eng), Ella Kim (Lattice CTO)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Sofia from Redwood. With me is Aaron, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya: Good, thanks. Sorry for the short delay, had to pull Miguel in. We're excited to dig into latency/throughput stuff.
[00:15] Sofia: Great. High level, this call is to understand your p95 targets, concurrency, streaming requirements and then propose hosted/dedicated/private options plus a benchmark plan.
[00:26] Aaron: Quick intro from me — I run bench infra for Redwood, mostly throughput/latency work, kernel selection, queueing and batching.
[00:34] Miguel: Awesome. I'll be owning infra integration and network stuff on our side.
[00:38] Ella: I'm here to scope the risk and cost side.

[01:05] Priya: So for context: we run Lattice Retail search+personalization, text generation for product descriptions and chat assist. Most critical is the chat assist with streaming UX — token-by-token. Our target is p95 under 300ms for short replies (<= 40 tokens). For longer generations we can accept higher p95 but need stable throughput.

[01:38] Aaron: Ok, that's helpful. When you say 300ms p95, is that entirely server-side or including network to your users?
[01:45] Priya: That's server-side. We measured client-to-edge at ~50-80ms; we want the inference p95 to be <300ms so overall UX is sub-400ms.

[02:10] Sofia: What's your concurrency profile? Steady state and burst?
[02:16] Priya: Steady is about 60 concurrent chat sessions, bursts up to 400 concurrent during promos. Avg tokens per request ~25-40, sometimes spikes to 200. Token rate during bursts ~12k tokens/sec.

[02:40] Aaron: Good to know. Do you need hard SLOs or more of a best-effort with fallbacks?
[02:45] Ella: We want predictability — if we pay for Dedicated we'd like SLA-backed latency targets. Hosted is fine for dev, but production we'd prefer predictable performance and data isolation.

[03:05] Sofia: Makes sense. We commonly propose Redwood Dedicated for that: reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput, autoscale and burst capacity. For the p95 targets you mentioned, key levers are model size, quantization, batching config, KV/prefix caching and routing policy.

[03:30] Aaron: Some live numbers — on H100, for a 7B LLM optimized with INT8 quant and Redwood runtime, short completions (<=40 tokens) tend to hit p95 ~120-180ms at low concurrency. At 100-200 concurrency that can creep up to 250-400ms depending on batching and streaming overhead.

[04:00] Priya: So you think 300ms p95 is realistic for 7B?
[04:04] Aaron: It's realistic at moderate concurrency if you tune batching and use prefix caching. Streaming adds overhead because we flush tokens earlier; that's typically +20-80ms depending on your chunk size.

[04:30] Miguel: How does KV cache/prefix cache help? We're worried about cold starts when different users ask different contexts.
[04:37] Aaron: Prefix caching stores key/value cache for recent prompts. If many requests share prefixes — for example, same system prompt or conversation preamble — we avoid recomputing attention keys which saves tokens/sec and reduces latency. For highly unique prompts it helps less. Cold starts show up in p95 and tail latency.

[05:05] Priya: Our chat has a fairly repeatable system prompt and templates, so prefix caching should be effective.

[05:14] Ella: Security questions — Dedicated vs Private: we need VPC peering and KMS integration. Also SOC2 + ISO are required for procurement.

[05:24] Sofia: We support VPC private deployments and customer-managed KMS for Private. Dedicated supports VPC peering and can be configured with KMS. We'll send SOC2 and ISO artifacts.

[05:45] Miguel: Network egress and perf is important. If we do Dedicated in the same region it's better, right?
[05:50] Aaron: Yes, colocating reduces network latency. We can route traffic regionally and fallback to other regions if capacity is constrained but that increases latency.

[06:10] Priya: Benchmarks — we want a realistic plan. Can you run token/sec and p95 under our prompt set?
[06:16] Aaron: Yes. Proposed benchmark: run three scenarios — 1) short chat (<=40 tokens) streaming enabled; 2) mid-length completion (100-200 tokens) non-streaming; 3) burst load (token/sec up to 12k) with mixed models. For each measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. We'll test hosted first, then Dedicated nodes provisioned for the trial.

[06:45] Sofia: We'll provide a benchmark script and a small harness. We'll need your sample prompts and traffic shape.

[07:00] Priya: We'll prepare 200 representative prompts and traffic profile.

[07:10] Miguel: Hardware question: A100 vs H100 — which do you recommend?
[07:13] Aaron: H100 has single-request latency benefits and better throughput for larger models; A100 is solid for cost-effective throughput. For 7B H100 gives lower p95 under heavy concurrency but costs more. We can show cost-latency tradeoffs in the pricing sheet.

[07:40] Ella: Model variants — are we talking 7B and 13B?
[07:44] Aaron: Yeah typical path: 7B for low-latency chat with INT8 quant; 13B if you need higher quality at cost of higher latency. We can also provide distilled/opt models or 4-bit/8-bit quant profiles.

[08:05] Priya: For our personalization quality we prefer 13B for the product description generator, but chat needs 7B to meet latency.

[08:20] Aaron: That aligns with what we usually see. Also consider split routing: route chat to low-latency 7B dedicated pool and longer gen to a separate capacity tier. Redwood supports policy-based routing and fallbacks.

[08:45] Miguel: How about batching? User-level streaming prevents larger batches, right?
[08:50] Aaron: Exactly. Streaming reduces batching window because you want tokens out quickly. We rely more on continuous batching and micro-batching. For token-by-token streaming we optimize kernel paths and reduce batching delay; still we can group tokens across requests if they align temporally.

[09:20] Priya: Any suggestions to reduce p95 without overprovisioning?

[09:23] Aaron: Yes — smaller model, quantization, prefix caching, tuned chunk size for streaming, reduce prompt size, and route repeatable flows to cached endpoints. Also horizontal capacity for bursts with autoscaling and controlled backpressure/fallback to cheaper models.

[10:00] Priya: Cost sensitivity — can you give a rough cost per 100k tokens for hosted vs dedicated?

[10:05] Sofia: We'll include detailed numbers in the pricing sheet but roughly hosted is higher per-token; Dedicated amortizes cost across reserved capacity so unit cost drops if you have steady usage. Private has platform fees plus infra costs.

[10:24] Ella: Procurement will ask for SOC2 and contract SLAs.

[10:28] Sofia: We'll attach compliance pack.

[10:45] Miguel: If we run the benchmark, how long before we get results?

[10:48] Aaron: Once we have prompts and traffic shape we can spin up a hosted run in 24-48 hours. For Dedicated trial nodes provisioning may take 2-5 business days depending on region.

[11:10] Priya: Streaming specifics: we care about token/second emitted to the client. We want smooth first-token time plus a steady token stream with small jitter.

[11:20] Aaron: We'll capture first-byte latency and effective token throughput. For streaming the token emission rate depends on model step latency and chunking; on optimized runtimes we often see consistent token/sec for short outputs but initial token can spike due to compute setup.

[11:50] Priya: Any gotchas re: prompt engineering affecting latency?

[11:55] Aaron: Long system prompts significantly increase per-token compute for some architectures because attention grows with sequence length. Try to keep system prompt concise or use reference tokens stored in prefix cache.

[12:10] Miguel: SLA granularity — can we get p95 SLOs per route?

[12:15] Sofia: Yes with Dedicated and enterprise Private we can set per-route SLOs and alerting. Hosted has best-effort SLOs and we publish performance profiles.

[12:35] Priya: How do fallbacks work if a Dedicated pool is saturated?

[12:38] Aaron: Smart routing can fall back to compatible variants — e.g., same model quantized or a lower capacity tier — with an automated policy. That keeps requests alive albeit with different latency/quality.

[13:05] Ella: About audit logs and RBAC?

[13:08] Sofia: Full audit logs, role-based access, and SSO/SAML are supported. Private gives you more control over log retention.

[13:30] Priya: Let's talk numbers — can you commit to a p95 under 300ms at 200 concurrent for 7B with streaming?

[13:36] Aaron: I won't commit without running benchmarks. Based on prior runs, on H100 with INT8 and prefix caching we can often meet ~200-280ms p95 at 200 concurrency for short streaming outputs, but results depend on prompt uniqueness and network. We'll validate with the benchmark.

[14:05] Miguel: For the benchmark, we should measure p50/p95/p99, first-byte, steady token/sec, and CPU/GPU utilization.

[14:12] Aaron: Agreed. Also measure cold vs warm cache performance and tail latencies.

[14:30] Priya: Any limitations for on-prem/private? We may need air-gapped later.

[14:34] Sofia: Private on-prem package supports air-gapped with an offline control plane; we have customers on that path but it's a longer onboarding and requires a different contract.

[15:00] Ella: Are there examples or case studies for similar retailers?

[15:03] Sofia: Yes, we'll share relevant case studies and benchmarks in the follow-up.

[15:20] Priya: Great. On rollout — can we start with hosted for dev, then Dedicated trial for prod?

[15:25] Sofia: That's our typical flow — dev on hosted, validate, then move to Dedicated with reserved capacity and SLA.

[15:40] Miguel: Any other infra constraints we should know about?

[15:43] Priya: We'll need to check VPC peering setup with our cloud team and any egress rules. Miguel will coordinate.

[16:00] Aaron: I'll draft the benchmark plan now — it will include config for concurrency (60 steady, 400 burst), token rates, chunk sizes for streaming, and model variants (7B/13B).

[16:18] Priya: Sounds good. Also include a cheap fallback plan — if p95 can't be met, how does routing degrade gracefully?

[16:23] Aaron: We'll include fallback policy examples: degrade to quantized variant or shorter generation, or queue with backpressure.

[16:40] Ella: Quick question — what telemetry do you expose so our SREs can monitor costs and latency?

[16:46] Sofia: Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency distributions, traces and error logs. We can set dashboard access for your team.

[17:05] Miguel: Ok next steps recap?

[17:08] Sofia: We'll send pricing, compliance pack and benchmark plan. You send prompts and traffic shape. Then schedule a deep-dive and run benchmarks (hosted first).

[17:20] Priya: That works. We'll aim to get prompts to you by 4/23.

[17:30] Sofia: Great. Thanks everyone.

[17:33] Ella: Thanks.

[17:35] Meeting ends.
